lessons.title: Water Requirements of Citrus Trees
lessons.body: Citrus trees need consistent moisture to produce good fruit, but the exact amount depends on tree age, soil, and climate. A mature orange tree in a warm area uses about 40 to 60 litres of water per day during peak summer. In cooler months, that drops to 15 to 25 litres. Young trees just planted need 5 to 10 litres every 2 to 3 days. The roots take up most water in the top 60 cm of soil, so you do not need to soak deeply beyond that. Sandy soils hold little water, so you may need to irrigate every day or two. Clay soils hold more but drain slowly, so water every 3 to 4 days. A simple test: dig a hole 30 cm deep near the tree. If the soil feels like a wrung-out sponge, moisture is good. If it crumbles dry, irrigate. If it drips water, you are overwatering. In Africa, many farmers use the 'bucket method' for young trees: punch a small hole in a 20-litre bucket, fill it, and let it drip slowly near the trunk. This gives about 20 litres over 4 to 6 hours. For mature trees, a common practice is to build a basin around the tree (1.5 m diameter) and fill it with 60 to 80 litres once a week in dry season. Always water in the early morning or late afternoon to reduce evaporation. Mulching with dry grass or crop residues around the base reduces water loss by up to 30%. Avoid wetting the trunk directly to prevent rot. Signs of too little water: leaves curl inward, fruit drops, and new growth stops. Signs of too much: yellowing leaves, root rot, and fungus on the trunk. Adjust based on what you see.

lessons.title: Drip Irrigation Design and Maintenance
lessons.body: Drip irrigation saves water by delivering it directly to the roots, drop by drop. For a small citrus orchard of 50 trees, you can build a simple system for under $200 using locally available materials. You need a water source (tank or borehole), a filter, a main line (32 mm PVC or black polyethylene), and drip lines (16 mm) with emitters spaced 60 cm apart. Each emitter puts out 2 to 4 litres per hour. For a mature tree, run 4 emitters per tree, each for 2 hours daily. That gives 16 to 32 litres per tree per day. Place emitters 30 cm from the trunk, under the canopy edge where feeder roots are densest. A filter is criticalâuse a screen filter (120 mesh) or sand filter to stop sand and debris clogging emitters. Flush the main line and drip lines every two weeks by opening the end caps for 2 minutes. Check emitters weekly: if flow is weak, remove the emitter and soak it in vinegar or a 1% chlorine solution for 30 minutes. In sandy soils, bury drip lines 10 cm deep to prevent damage from animals and sun. In clay soils, lay them on the surface and cover with mulch. Pressure matters: keep it at 1 to 1.5 bar. Too low and water does not reach the end; too high and fittings burst. Use a pressure gauge at the filter. For a 1-hectare orchard, you need about 400 to 600 metres of drip line. A common mistake is not installing a valve for each blockâdivide your orchard into 2 or 3 blocks so you can water one at a time if pressure is low. Maintenance is simple: check for leaks, clean filters weekly, and replace damaged emitters. With good care, drip lines last 5 to 8 years.

lessons.title: Sprinkler and Micro-Sprinkler Systems
lessons.body: Sprinklers spray water over the whole orchard, while micro-sprinklers are smaller and wet only the area under the tree. For citrus, micro-sprinklers are better because they keep the trunk dry and reduce disease. A micro-sprinkler puts out 30 to 60 litres per hour and covers a circle of 1.5 to 2 metres. You need one micro-sprinkler per mature tree, placed 30 cm from the trunk. Run it for 30 to 60 minutes daily in peak season. For young trees, use one micro-sprinkler with a smaller flow rate (20 to 30 litres per hour) for 20 minutes. Sprinklers are useful for frost protection in cold areas, but they wet the canopy and can cause fungal problems. If you use sprinklers, choose impact sprinklers with a low trajectory (25 degrees) to reduce evaporation. Space them 12 m by 12 m for full coverage. You need about 3 to 4 bar pressure for sprinklers, which may require a pump. Micro-sprinklers need only 1 to 2 bar. In Africa, many farmers use a 'micro-sprinkler on a stake' system: a small plastic sprinkler on a 30 cm stake, connected to a 16 mm line. This is cheap and easy to move. Maintenance: check for clogged nozzles every week. Soak them in vinegar if blocked. Replace worn parts. In windy areas, micro-sprinklers are better because wind blows sprinkler water off-target. A good rule: if you see dry patches under the tree, adjust the sprinkler or add another. For a 1-hectare orchard, you need about 100 to 150 micro-sprinklers. Cost is roughly $1 to $2 per unit. Always water early morning or evening to cut evaporation losses by up to 40%. Avoid overhead sprinklers in areas with high humidity or known fungal diseases.

lessons.title: Scheduling Irrigation Based on Evapotranspiration
lessons.body: Evapotranspiration (ET) is the water lost from soil evaporation and plant transpiration. By knowing ET, you water exactly what the tree uses. In Africa, you can get ET data from local weather stations or use a simple 'pan evaporation' method. Place a Class A evaporation pan (a shallow metal pan 1.2 m diameter) near your orchard. Measure the water level daily. The ET for citrus is about 0.7 times the pan evaporation. So if the pan loses 8 mm of water in a day, your citrus uses about 5.6 mm. To convert mm to litres per tree: multiply mm by the tree's canopy area. For a tree with 2 m canopy diameter, area is about 3.14 mÂ². So 5.6 mm x 3.14 = 17.6 litres per tree per day. For a mature tree with 4 m canopy, area is 12.6 mÂ², so 5.6 x 12.6 = 70 litres. You can also use a simple 'ET gauge' made from a plastic bottle with a ruler, but the pan method is more accurate. If you cannot measure ET, use the 'feel method': after irrigation, wait 2 days, dig 30 cm down. If soil is dry, you waited too long. If wet, you can wait another day. Another method: install a tensiometer (a $30 device) at 30 cm depth. Irrigate when it reads -40 to -60 kPa for sandy soil, or -60 to -80 kPa for clay. Keep a simple notebook: date, pan evaporation, litres applied. After one season, you will see a pattern. In dry season, you may irrigate every day; in rainy season, skip. This saves water and money. Overwatering wastes water and leaches nutrients. Underwatering stresses trees and reduces yield. ET scheduling is the most scientific way to get it right.

lessons.title: Water Quality and Salinity Management
lessons.body: Not all water is good for citrus. High salt, high sodium, or high chloride can damage trees. Citrus is moderately sensitive to salinity. If your water has more than 1,000 ppm (parts per million) of total dissolved salts, you may see leaf burn, stunted growth, and small fruit. You can test water at a local agricultural office or with a cheap EC meter ($20). EC (electrical conductivity) above 1.5 dS/m is risky. Sodium above 3 meq/L and chloride above 4 meq/L can cause toxicity. In coastal areas or near boreholes, salinity is common. To manage salinity: first, leach the soil by applying extra water (10-20% more than ET) to push salts below the root zone. Do this every 3 to 4 irrigations. Second, add gypsum (calcium sulfate) at 1 to 2 tonnes per hectare to replace sodium on soil particles. Third, choose rootstocks that tolerate salt, such as Cleopatra mandarin or Rough lemon. Fourth, avoid overhead sprinklers with salty waterâsalt burns leaves. Use drip or micro-sprinklers instead. Fifth, mulch heavily to reduce evaporation, which concentrates salts. If your water is very salty (EC > 3 dS/m), consider mixing with rainwater from a tank. In Africa, many farmers collect rainwater from roofs into tanks and use it for young trees. Test your water at least once a year. A simple field test: put a drop of water on a clean glass slide, let it dry. If a white crust remains, salts are present. For a more precise test, use a TDS meter. Remember: prevention is cheaper than cure. If you see salt crust on soil surface, act immediately. Leach, add gypsum, and switch to drip irrigation.

lessons.title: Drought Mitigation Strategies
lessons.body: Drought is a reality in many parts of Africa. But you can keep citrus alive and productive with smart strategies. First, reduce water loss. Mulch every tree with a 10 cm layer of dry grass, straw, or crop residues. This cuts evaporation by 30-50%. Keep the mulch 10 cm away from the trunk to prevent rot. Second, prune severely in drought years. Remove 30-40% of the canopy to reduce water demand. Do this at the start of dry season. Third, use shade nets (30-50% shade) over young trees. This reduces water use by 20-30%. Fourth, harvest water. Dig contour trenches or 'swales' between tree rows to capture runoff. A 30 cm deep trench, 50 cm wide, can hold 150 litres per metre. Fill trenches with stones or mulch to slow evaporation. Fifth, use deficit irrigation. Instead of full water, apply 50-70% of normal ET. This keeps trees alive but reduces yield. It is better than losing trees. Sixth, choose drought-tolerant rootstocks like Rough lemon, Volckameriana, or Cleopatra mandarin. Seventh, if you have a borehole, install a solar pump. A 300-watt solar panel can pump 1,000 litres per day from 10 m depth. This is cheaper than diesel. Eighth, reuse greywater from household sinks and showers. Do not use water with bleach or strong soap. Ninth, plant windbreaks (e.g., moringa or casuarina) to reduce wind evaporation. Tenth, monitor trees daily. If leaves roll in the morning, irrigate immediately. If you have very little water, prioritise young trees and heavy bearers. In extreme drought, you may need to remove fruit to save the tree. Remember: a tree that survives drought will recover; a dead tree is a total loss. Plan ahead: store water in tanks during rainy season. A 5,000-litre tank can carry a small orchard through 2 months of drought.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Water Management and Irrigation for Citrus in Africa

Water is the single most controllable input determining citrus yield, fruit size, and rind quality in African orchards. In most commercial citrus operations across South Africa, Morocco, Egypt, Zimbabwe, and Tanzania, irrigation accounts for 25â45% of total production costs. This practical reference gives you the numbers, schedules, and field checks you need to make irrigation decisions that protect both your crop and your margin.

Why Water Management Drives Profit

Citrus is a deep-rooted evergreen. Unlike annual crops, it carries fruit and canopy simultaneously, so water stress at any stage has compounding effects: reduced fruit set, smaller fruit, poor juice content, and increased susceptibility to pests. Conversely, over-irrigation leaches nitrogen (a direct cash loss), raises water tables, and promotes root rot. The business case is simple: every cubic metre of water must produce measurable fruit. In South Africa, citrus growers on the Lower Olifants River report that moving from flood to drip irrigation cut water use by 30â40% while increasing marketable yield by 8â15%.

Water Requirements of Citrus Trees

Citrus evapotranspiration (ETc) is calculated as ETc = ETo Ã Kc, where ETo is reference evapotranspiration and Kc is the crop coefficient. For mature citrus, Kc ranges from 0.6 (winter) to 0.8 (peak summer). A mature orchard in a warm, dry African climate typically needs 900â1,300 mm of water per year. In the Western Cape (Mediterranean climate), that drops to 700â900 mm; in the Lowveld (subtropical), it rises to 1,200â1,400 mm. Young trees need 20â40 litres per week in year one, rising to 150â300 litres per week by year four.

Drip Irrigation Design and Maintenance

Drip is the default choice for new citrus plantings in Africa because it delivers water directly to the root zone, reduces weed pressure, and allows fertigation. Design parameters: one or two emitters per tree, 2â4 L/h each, spaced 0.5â1.0 m apart on the lateral. For a 5 m Ã 5 m spacing (400 trees/ha), you need 800â1,600 emitters/ha. A typical block of 1 ha requires a flow rate of 8â16 mÂ³/h at 1.5â2.0 bar. Laterals should be 16 mm or 20 mm, with a maximum run length of 80â120 m depending on slope.

Maintenance is where most African growers lose money. Clogged emitters cause uneven growth, small fruit, and tree death. The three killers are: (1) physical particles (sand, silt), (2) chemical precipitates (calcium carbonate, iron), and (3) biological growth (algae, bacteria). Flush laterals every two weeks, inject chlorine (1â2 ppm free chlorine) monthly, and acidify with hydrochloric or nitric acid when pH exceeds 7.5. Install a sand filter and a screen filter (120 mesh) at the pump. Budget 5â8% of irrigation capital cost annually for maintenance.

Sprinkler and Micro-Sprinkler Systems

Micro-sprinklers (also called micro-jets) are common in sandy soils and on slopes where drip laterals are impractical. They wet 30â50% of the soil surface, which helps leach salts below the root zone â a major advantage in North Africa and the Middle East. A micro-sprinkler delivers 30â70 L/h, covering a 1.5â2.5 m diameter. For mature trees, one micro-sprinkler per tree at 40 L/h is standard. Overhead sprinklers are used for frost protection and heat stress relief, but they increase disease pressure (especially citrus canker and black spot) and waste water through evaporation. In windy African conditions, overhead sprinkler efficiency can drop to 60â70%.

Scheduling Irrigation Based on Evapotranspiration

ET-based scheduling is the gold standard. You can get daily ETo data from local weather stations, the FAO Penman-Monteith method, or free online tools like the South African Agricultural Research Council (ARC) weather network. The calculation: Irrigation requirement (mm) = ETo Ã Kc â effective rainfall. Then convert to litres per tree: multiply by the canopy area and divide by the wetted area. For a 5 m Ã 5 m spacing, 1 mm of water = 25 litres per tree (if the wetted area is the full square). With drip, only 30â40% of the soil surface is wetted, so you apply less water but more frequently â typically every 1â3 days in summer.

Use soil moisture sensors (capacitance or tensiometers) at 30 cm and 60 cm depth to verify your schedule. The rule: never let soil moisture drop below 60% of field capacity during fruit set and fruit sizing. Table 1 shows typical irrigation schedules for three African citrus regions.

Table 1: Typical Citrus Irrigation Requirements by African Region (mature orchard, 400 trees/ha)
Region Climate Annual ETo (mm) Annual ETc (mm) Peak Summer (L/tree/day) Winter (L/tree/day)
Western Cape, South Africa Mediterranean 1,200â1,400 700â900 40â60 5â15
Lowveld, South Africa / Zimbabwe Subtropical 1,500â1,800 1,000â1,300 60â90 15â25
Souss-Massa, Morocco Arid Mediterranean 1,600â2,000 1,100â1,400 70â100 20â30
Nile Delta, Egypt Hot desert 1,800â2,200 1,200â1,500 80â110 25â35

Source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Allen et al., 1998); DAFF (South Africa) citrus production guidelines; Moroccan Ministry of Agriculture (INRA) citrus water requirements.

Water Quality and Salinity Management

Citrus is moderately sensitive to salinity. Yield loss begins when soil electrical conductivity (ECe) exceeds 1.4 dS/m, and severe losses occur above 4.0 dS/m. In North Africa and the Middle East, irrigation water with EC above 1.5 dS/m requires leaching and careful variety selection. Chloride and sodium are the main culprits â they accumulate in leaf margins and cause tip burn. Table 2 shows water quality thresholds.

Table 2: Irrigation Water Quality Guidelines for Citrus
Parameter Safe Moderate Risk High Risk Action Required
EC (dS/m) < 0.7 0.7â1.5 > 1.5 Leach 15â20% extra water; monitor leaf chloride
Chloride (mg/L) < 140 140â250 > 250 Switch to drip; avoid overhead sprinklers
Sodium (mg/L) < 115 115â200 > 200 Apply gypsum; improve drainage
Boron (mg/L) < 0.5 0.5â1.0 > 1.0 Leach; use tolerant rootstocks (e.g., Carrizo)

Source: FAO Water Quality for Agriculture (Ayers & Westcot, 1985); University of California DANR Publication 3372; South African Water Research Commission (WRC) irrigation guidelines.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â CHEMICAL INJECTION AND WATER TREATMENT

Injecting chlorine, acid, or fertiliser into irrigation lines is hazardous. Always use a backflow prevention device (air gap or reduced-pressure zone valve) to protect drinking water sources. Never mix chlorine and acid â toxic chlorine gas can be released. Wear chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and a respirator when handling concentrated acids or chlorine. Store chemicals in a locked, ventilated shed away from children and livestock. In Africa, where rural water supplies are often shared, backflow protection is not optional â it is a legal and moral requirement.

Drought Mitigation Strategies

Drought is the biggest climate risk for African citrus. Mitigation is both agronomic and financial. Agronomically: (1) apply mulch (straw, compost, or plastic) to reduce evaporation by 20â30%; (2) use deficit irrigation during less critical stages (post-harvest) â but never during flowering or fruit sizing; (3) install shade nets (20â30% shade) to cut ETc by 15â25%; (4) select drought-tolerant rootstocks such as Rough Lemon, Volkameriana, or Carrizo Citrange; (5) maintain ground cover with cover crops to improve infiltration. Financially: (1) build a farm dam or reservoir to store winter rainfall; (2) join a water users association to secure allocations; (3) invest in soil moisture monitoring to avoid over-irrigation; (4) consider crop insurance or diversification into drought-tolerant crops on marginal blocks.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Check soil moisture daily at 30 cm and 60 cm depth during summer â never let it drop below 60% field capacity.
  • Calculate ETc weekly using local ETo data and Kc values (0.6â0.8 for citrus). Adjust for rainfall.
  • Flush drip laterals every 14 days and clean filters weekly. Clogged emitters are silent profit killers.
  • Test irrigation water annually for EC, chloride, sodium, and boron. Act on moderate-risk results before yield drops.
  • Apply mulch around tree basins to cut evaporation and suppress weeds.
  • Monitor leaf chloride every 3 months if using water above 1.0 dS/m. Tip burn means yield loss.
  • Maintain backflow prevention and safe chemical handling â protect your family and community.
  • Keep a water budget â record every irrigation event, rainfall, and yield outcome. Data drives better decisions next season.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56: Crop Evapotranspiration â the global standard for ETc calculation.
  • FAO Water Quality for Agriculture (Ayers & Westcot, 1985) â salinity and water quality thresholds.
  • South African Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (DAFF) â citrus production guidelines and irrigation manuals.
  • Agricultural Research Council (ARC), South Africa â weather data, soil moisture tools, and citrus research.
  • Water Research Commission (WRC), South Africa â free irrigation and water management reports.

Bottom line: Water management is not a technical afterthought â it is a business discipline. Measure, schedule, maintain, and record. Every litre you save is a litre you can sell as fruit. In Africa's variable climate, the growers who treat water as a managed asset will still be farming when the drought years come.

quiz.q: How much water does a mature orange tree use per day in peak summer?
quiz.explanation: A mature orange tree in a warm area uses about 40 to 60 litres per day during peak summer.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to check if young citrus trees need water?
options: A) Dig a hole 30 cm deep and feel the soil
B) Wait for leaves to turn yellow
D) Count the number of leaves
quiz.explanation: Digging a hole and feeling the soil moisture is a practical field test.

quiz.q: Which mulch material is recommended to reduce evaporation around citrus trees?
options: B) Dry grass or crop residues
quiz.explanation: Dry grass or crop residues are commonly used and effective mulches.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for emitters on a drip line for citrus?
quiz.explanation: Emitters are typically spaced 60 cm apart on the drip line.

quiz.q: How often should you flush drip lines?
quiz.explanation: Flushing every two weeks prevents clogging from debris and sediment.

quiz.q: What is the ideal pressure for a drip irrigation system?
quiz.explanation: Drip systems operate best at 1 to 1.5 bar pressure.

quiz.q: How many emitters are recommended per mature citrus tree in a drip system?
quiz.explanation: Four emitters per mature tree are typical to provide adequate coverage.

quiz.q: What is a common problem with sprinkler irrigation for citrus?
options: A) It saves too much water
B) It wets the canopy and can cause fungal diseases
D) It cannot be used in Africa
quiz.explanation: Wetting the canopy increases the risk of fungal problems.

quiz.q: What flow rate does a typical micro-sprinkler have?
quiz.explanation: Micro-sprinklers usually emit 30 to 60 litres per hour.

quiz.q: Why are micro-sprinklers preferred over overhead sprinklers in windy areas?
options: B) They are less affected by wind
D) They cover a larger area
quiz.explanation: Micro-sprinklers apply water closer to the ground, so wind drift is minimal.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of a micro-sprinkler unit?
quiz.explanation: Micro-sprinklers typically cost between $1 and $2 each.

quiz.q: How many micro-sprinklers are needed for a 1-hectare citrus orchard?
quiz.explanation: About 100 to 150 micro-sprinklers are needed per hectare.

quiz.q: What is evapotranspiration (ET)?
options: A) Water lost from soil and plants
B) Water stored in the soil
quiz.explanation: ET is the combined water loss from soil evaporation and plant transpiration.

quiz.q: How do you convert pan evaporation to citrus ET?
quiz.explanation: Citrus ET is about 0.7 times the pan evaporation.

quiz.q: If a pan loses 8 mm of water, what is the approximate ET for citrus?
For a tree with a 2 m canopy diameter, what is the canopy area?
quiz.explanation: Area = ÏrÂ², r = 1 m, so area = 3.14 mÂ².

quiz.q: What device can be used to measure soil moisture tension?
quiz.explanation: A tensiometer measures soil moisture tension in kPa.

quiz.q: At what tensiometer reading should you irrigate sandy soil?
quiz.explanation: For sandy soil, irrigate when the tensiometer reads -40 to -60 kPa.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended EC of irrigation water for citrus?
quiz.explanation: EC above 1.5 dS/m is risky for citrus.

quiz.q: Which rootstock is tolerant to salinity?
quiz.explanation: Cleopatra mandarin is known for salt tolerance.

quiz.q: How much gypsum is recommended to manage sodium in soil?
quiz.explanation: Apply 1 to 2 tonnes of gypsum per hectare to replace sodium.

quiz.q: What is a simple field test for salinity?
options: B) Let a drop of water dry on a glass slide and look for white crust
quiz.explanation: A white crust after drying indicates salts.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid overhead sprinklers with salty water?
quiz.explanation: Salt accumulation on leaves causes leaf burn.

quiz.q: How much can mulch reduce evaporation?
quiz.explanation: Mulch can cut evaporation by 30 to 50%.

quiz.q: What is deficit irrigation?
options: A) Applying more water than ET
quiz.explanation: Deficit irrigation applies less water than full ET to save water.

quiz.q: Which of these is a drought-tolerant rootstock?
quiz.explanation: Rough lemon is known for drought tolerance.

quiz.q: How much water can a 300-watt solar pump lift per day from 10 m depth?
quiz.explanation: A 300-watt solar pump can pump about 1,000 litres per day from 10 m.

quiz.q: What is a recommended windbreak tree for citrus orchards?
quiz.explanation: Moringa is commonly used as a windbreak in Africa.

quiz.q: When should you irrigate if leaves are rolling in the morning?
quiz.explanation: Leaf rolling in the morning indicates severe water stress; irrigate immediately.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of contour trenches in drought mitigation?
quiz.explanation: Contour trenches capture and store runoff for trees to use.
